items.text: The service worker loads its own Workbox runtime, served from the same origin. Scanning this same file for absolute URLs guarantees no external origin is referenced in it.

Opens the vault once for the whole application and makes it available.
*
The subscription goes through `useSyncExternalStore`: the vault reports its
changes with a plain callback, knowing nothing about React. That is what
lets `src/core` stay an ordinary TypeScript library, testable without a
render.

A stand-in for `emoji-mart`, substituted at build time.
*
The emoji-picker library fetches its localisation data *and* its images
from a CDN, at runtime. That is incompatible with Nook's promise: the CSP
would block those requests, and the picker would be silently broken — the
worst of the two situations, since the user would see a feature that does
not work without knowing why.
*
Disabling it with an option was not enough: the code still went into the
served files, and would have stayed there at the mercy of a future setting.
An alias in `vite.config.ts` therefore replaces it with this module, and
the network guard observes its absence.
*
What is lost: the emoji menu triggered by typing ":". Emoji typed on the
system keyboard work normally.
*
This module stands in for `emoji-mart` and for `@emoji-mart/data` alike: the
first reads functions, the second a data object, and the empty default
export suits both.

Confirmation of a destructive action.
*
Built on the native `<dialog>`, which gives — correctly, and for free —
focus trapping, Escape to close, an inert backdrop and the right semantics
for screen readers. Reimplementing all of that by hand is the shortcut that
produces modals nobody can use from a keyboard.

One focus treatment across the whole application. It is visible on light
and dark backgrounds alike because it uses the accent, never a browser
default hue.
